walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme F: Religion, Human Rights & Social Justice — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme F: Religion, Human Rights & Social Justice brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme F: Religion, Human Rights & Social Justice.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Jesus was half God and half human.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

mcqs.q: What does utilitarianism say is right action?
options: The action that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number — judged by consequences, not intentions or rules.
Utilitarianism says you should always tell the truth.
Whatever makes you personally happy is the right thing to do.
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Hinduism worships no gods, only ancestors.
Hinduism is straightforwardly polytheistic with millions of separate gods.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
It is more accurately described as henotheistic or monistic — many gods (devas) are considered aspects or manifestations of one ultimate reality (Brahman).
